**Treat research as a sequence of evidence-building steps.** A research agent has to decide what it needs to know, retrieve information, compare sources, resolve discrepancies, and produce an answer supported by that evidence. Calling a search tool repeatedly is not itself a research strategy. The output should preserve which source supports which conclusion.

**A concrete example.** For “compare three battery technologies for a cold-weather device,” first identify decision criteria such as operating temperature, energy density, lifetime, and cost. Search for each criterion using authoritative sources, record dates and measurement conditions, then compare like with like. A laboratory maximum at room temperature is not directly comparable to a commercial product's guaranteed cold-temperature specification.

**Why durable state matters.** A long job may pause, retry, or lose a worker. Store the question, current plan, collected evidence, unresolved claims, and remaining budget outside the model's transient context. On restart, the system should continue from known state instead of repeating searches or silently forgetting contradictions. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)

Parallel research can help independent subquestions, but merging results requires deduplication and reconciliation. More workers can also repeat the same sources or amplify an early mistaken assumption. Evaluate final evidence coverage and factual accuracy rather than rewarding the number of tool calls.

**Define a stopping condition.** Stop when the required claims have sufficient evidence or the time/budget limit is reached. Clearly separate established findings from unresolved questions. An agent that always keeps researching is not useful, and one that stops after the first convenient source may be confidently incomplete.

**Technical details and references.**

Represent a research job as a durable state machine containing the user objective, constraints, plan, evidence records, remaining time/token budget, and pending tool calls. Ask a clarifying question when an unresolved choice would change the research scope or produce an unusable result; do not ask for facts retrievable from permitted sources.

A planner decomposes the objective into evidence-seeking questions. Execute independent searches concurrently under bounded fan-out, deduplicate URLs, and retain source dates, excerpts, and citation IDs. The controller decides whether another search can close a specific evidence gap; cap depth, tool count, retries, and spend. Retrieved pages are untrusted evidence, not instructions to the agent. Tool credentials and side-effect permissions remain outside model control.

Compact context into claims, supporting evidence IDs, contradictions, and unfinished questions rather than discarding provenance. For an illustrative 60-second interactive budget, reserve time for synthesis and allow only bounded research waves; offer a resumable background job for larger requests. Evaluate factual support, coverage, contradiction handling, completion rate, and cost per successful task. A timeout should return a clearly partial report with preserved evidence, not a fabricated conclusion.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** Treat each tool step as a state transition $s_{t+1}=F(s_t,a_t,o_t)$ recorded durably. Retry read operations safely and attach idempotency keys or approval gates to externally consequential writes. Evaluate final evidence quality and task completion under a fixed budget, since more tool calls can increase cost and error exposure without improving the result. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system) and [2](https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/).
